paper_title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: https://zhixuanli.github.io/projects/li2026protocast

Data-driven weather forecasting uses historical multivariate observations to predict future meteorological fields. Forecasting models aim to capture both spatial relationships and temporal evolution. Pangu-Weather [2] and GraphCast [18] demonstrate progress in data-driven weather prediction. Within weather field, different locations exhibit distinct states and evolution patterns. Forecasting models therefore need to distinguish these local evolution patterns. Making their influence on predictions explicit also helps interpret model behavior. Representative Transformer forecasters such as Earthformer [10] and PredFormer [38] model these spatial relationships and local evolution patterns through spatiotemporal attention. However, the learned patterns remain implicit in features and parameters, as illustrated in Figure 1(a). This makes it difficult to trace which representative patterns influence predictions at particular location. Additionally, if these local evolution patterns are not adequately distinguished, the model can produce similar forecasts for states that develop differently, increasing prediction error. To support this distinction, explicit references in the form of prototypes can help relate local states to representative patterns. common use of these references is to guide sampleor task-level prediction, as illustrated in Figure 1(b). For example, ProtoPNet [6] aggregates similarities between image parts and prototypes into image-level classification evidence, while ProtoTS [27] combines hierarchical temporal prototypes to construct future sequences. HyperAdapter [40] uses task prototypes to generate adapter parameters. However, using prototype information at the sample or task level leaves open how different positions within weather field should be updated according to their own evolution. Different locations can follow different trajectories even when their present states are similar. At the same location, meteorological variables also exhibit distinct but interdependent dynamics. To realize this adaptation, we propose ProtoCast, spatiotemporal forecasting framework that retains distinct representations and prototype banks for meteorological variable groups. As illustrated in Figure 1(c), each group shares its prototype bank across locations, while local evolution determines the prototype mixture used at each location. Our design combines group-specific low-rank residual corrections with cross-variable interactions before and after correction. Tracked prototype refitting preserves the association between pattern references and learned correction operators during joint training. Specifically, first, group-specific encoders retain separate variable representations, while shared temporal and spatial blocks model their evolution. Pre-correction attention supplies cross-variable context at each patch and lead. Second, evolution-aware descriptors combine history, temporal change, and forecast context to select sparse prototype mixtures. The associated low-rank operators produce group-specific residual corrections. Gated attention exchanges corrected features across groups before final spatial processing and group-specific decoding. Finally, joint training updates the network and correction operators, while epoch-wise refitting and slot tracking preserve prototypeoperator associations. We introduce ProtoCast with group-specific representations and prototype banks alongside shared spatiotemporal modeling. Evolution-aware matching adapts features to distinct dynamics across locations and variable groups. We combine sparse mixtures of prototype-specific lowrank corrections with cross-variable interactions before and after correction. Tracked refitting preserves prototype-operator associations, making local corrections more interpretable. Among the compared methods, ProtoCast ranks first on 13 of the 16 metrics on GlobalForecast and all 16 metrics on TyphoonTracking. Prototype deletion reveals how individual local corrections affect forecast accuracy. 2. Related Work 2.1. Spatiotemporal Weather Forecasting Data-driven weather forecasting explores spatial representations and multi-step prediction. FourCastNet [26] and SFNO [4] use Fourier operators, while Pangu-Weather [2] and GraphCast [18] use 3D Transformers and multiscale graph networks. FuXi [8] and FengWu [7] reduce longerrange errors through range-specific cascaded models and 2 replayed predictions, respectively. Stormer [25] combines interval randomization and pressure-weighted losses, while NeuralGCM [16] couples differentiable atmospheric dynamics with learned parameterizations. GenCast [29] generates diffusion-based ensembles, and ATLAS [17] combines downsampled latents with history-conditioned local projection for probabilistic forecasting. ClimaX [24] aggregates variables for weather and climate transfer, and Aurora [3] learns unified 3D representations from diverse Earth-system data. WeatherNext 3 [32] incorporates satellite observations for hourly forecasts and learns precipitation, cyclone, and station targets. Related spatiotemporal models use convolutional recurrence [34], convolutional temporal modeling [11], and attention in Earthformer [10] and PredFormer [38]. These architectures capture local variation, but their learned evolution patterns remain implicit in distributed representations. ProtoCast provides explicit group-specific prototype references for local feature correction. Each variable group follows its own dynamics while exchanging information across groups for multivariate forecasting. 2.2. Prototype Learning in Meteorology Prototype learning grounds prediction in shared class references [35] or visual parts [6, 9, 22, 23, 33]. These methods connect prototype matches to classification evidence through similarities, tree decisions, or sparse weights. ProtoTS [27] combines hierarchical temporal prototypes for sequence forecasting. subseasonal-to-seasonal In meteorology, ProtoLNet [1] uses location-scaled matching to identify Madden-Julian oscillation phases. Its application [12] predicts temperature-anomaly classes using precipitation-anomaly prototypes, transferring the model from CESM2 to ERA5. Mechanism Learning [14] combines historical queries and prototypes into forecasting representations. These methods form class evidence or forecast representations. Prototype-based HyperAdapter [40] generates adapter parameters from task prototypes and layer information through hypernetwork, but selecting single prototype when adapting to new task can leave useful information from other prototypes unused. ProtoCast matches evolving local states to separate variable-group prototype banks and combines multiple low-rank correction operators within the forecasting network. Cross-variable context informs matching, and gated fusion exchanges corrected features before prediction. Joint Training and Tracked Prototype Refitting As the forecasting network learns, the features used for prototype matching change. Maintaining this association lets updated prototype references reuse their learned correction operators across epochs. Experiments To interpret local correction, we need to identify which matched patterns contributed to it and how they affected the features. We therefore decompose the residual before post-correction fusion into weighted prototype contributions r(g) ℓ,n,k. Each contribution combines its matching weight with the corresponding low-rank operator response. The weights identify relevant patterns, while residual vectors give their contributions at each forecast lead. Training patches with high query-to-prototype similarity characterize the associated historical evolution. We interpret local corrections by tracing the matched prototypes, their weighted residual contributions, and the forecast changes caused by removing individual contributions. To examine its effect on prediction, we remove selected contribution r(g) ℓ,n,k from (cid:101)H and recompute the subsequent layers.
